summary: Turns a touchscreen terminal into a single-purpose appliance: two fixed pages, no address bar, and nothing to wander off into.
description: A browser on a factory floor is a liability. It has an address bar, a back button to somewhere it should not be, and a settings screen an operator can reach by accident. Robot Browser has none of that: it shows the two pages a terminal is for - the transaction page your SCADA server serves, and the terminal's own web interface - and it is very difficult to leave.

Everything a terminal needs is on the terminal. WiFi setup, wired addressing, the time server, system information and the SCADA connection state are one tap away on a toolbar sized for gloved hands, with an on-screen keyboard that needs no keyboard attached. A terminal whose network has died can be fixed where it stands.

Mark a terminal secure on the server and it asks who is there before showing anything. A worker presents a card, scans a badge or keys their code; the terminal checks with the server, opens their session, and closes it the moment the terminal is left alone. Signing off is not something anyone has to remember.
highlights: An operator sets the text size at the terminal, in Info, with the page resizing as they press
The size is remembered per terminal and re-applied after every load, so it survives Home, Remote, a reload and a restart
WB_PAGE_ZOOM sets the size a deployment starts at, for a fleet that already knows its panels
Dialog buttons and their labels fit an 800x480 panel instead of keeping desktop padding
requires: A GPU and a compositor - X11 or Wayland. QtWebEngine cannot run on a plain framebuffer.
NetworkManager, for the WiFi and wired network screens.
robot-scada-client, for the server status, the station name and secure sign-on.
wsrobot, to sign on with a card or a scanned badge.

features.title: Two fixed pages
features.detail: Transaction page and local web UI on dedicated buttons. No address bar, no history, nowhere to wander.

features.title: Sized for whoever is reading it
features.detail: The remote page is somebody else's, laid out for a desk. An operator makes it bigger from the toolbar, and the terminal remembers.

features.title: Sign-on by card, badge or code
features.detail: RFID cards, scanned barcodes and keypad codes all reach the same check against your SCADA server.

features.title: Locks itself, signs them off
features.detail: An unattended terminal locks after a set time and closes the worker's session, including at shutdown.

features.title: Network setup built in
features.detail: WiFi scanning and connection, wired IP configuration and a time server, all from the toolbar.

features.title: Server status at a glance
features.detail: The SCADA connection, the station name and the last contact time, without leaving the page.

features.title: On-screen keyboard
features.detail: Three layouts sized for the panel it runs on, from a 7-inch terminal to a 19-inch panel PC.

features.title: Managed from the server
features.detail: Which pages it shows, whether it locks and which application runs are set centrally and applied without a visit.

features.title: Build pages without hardware
features.detail: Developer profiles reproduce each terminal's exact viewport on a PC, so a page can be laid out before a terminal exists.

notes: A secure terminal needs its server: with the network down, nobody signs on. That is deliberate - a terminal that cannot check is a terminal that cannot know.
Staff sign-in with a username and password is not built yet. Worker sign-on is.
The text size is per terminal, not per operator. A terminal is shared, and a size that changed with whoever signed on would be a size nobody could rely on.
